paragraphs: The following assessments concern how magnetic resonance imaging technologists perform imaging examinations. They do not predict hiring, qualifications, licensure, or contract outcomes.

The core work of magnetic resonance imaging technologists is to safely complete MRI examinations as ordered and ensure image quality: check orders and examination sites, screen for contraindications such as internal metal, pacemakers, artificial heart valves, pregnancy, and tattoos, explain procedures to patients and position and immobilize them, select coils and imaging techniques, operate MRI scanners to acquire images, administer intravenous gadolinium contrast when needed within scope of practice, connect physiological monitoring leads, check image quality, calibrate equipment and troubleshoot, back up and produce image records and report to physicians, schedule appointments, and inventory supplies.

Entirely fictional task package: provide a fictional MRI examination order and patient screening checklist, including 1 contraindication screening form and 1 image quality abnormality. Within 60 minutes, write screening points, positioning and coil choices, contrast and monitoring boundaries, image quality checks, and abnormality escalation steps. Do not use real patient, image, or institution data.

Sample output and reflection: check whether you first verified orders and contraindications, specified positioning and coils, explained contrast and monitoring boundaries, and provided handling and escalation paths for image quality abnormalities. Then ask whether you can remain rigorous under patient safety requirements and time pressure, and whether you are willing to take responsibility for patient safety and image quality.

This page covers O*NET29-2035.00 MRI technologists: acquiring images under medical orders and approved protocols, checking technical image quality and patient safety, communicating, and documenting. O*NET explicitly limits medication administration tasks to scope of practice. Technologists are not diagnostic radiologists, and a job title does not confer authority to administer medication or sedation or sign diagnostic reports.

entries: Inputs: physician orders and examination requests, patients and medical histories, contraindication screening forms for metal / implants / pregnancy / tattoos, MRI scanners and coils, gadolinium contrast and intravenous administration equipment, physiological monitoring leads and PAC units, image workstations and storage media, supplies, and record forms.

Inspectable outputs: MRI images meeting quality requirements, correct patient positioning and coil settings, contraindication screening and informed communication records, contrast administration and monitoring records, equipment calibration and troubleshooting records, image backups and films / records, and appointment and supply records.

Complete workflow: check orders and examination sites → screen for contraindications and collect medical history → explain procedures and position and immobilize the patient → select coils and imaging techniques → operate the scanner to acquire images and connect monitoring → check image quality and investigate abnormalities → back up / produce images, report, and document.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether contraindication and safety conditions are satisfied, whether positioning and coils are appropriate, whether image quality meets requirements, whether contrast is needed within scope of practice, when to reassure patients or request sedation, and how to stop and escalate equipment or patient abnormalities.

Patient contact, equipment operation, and scheduling collaboration in hospitals and imaging centers; check posture and shifts for the specific job. O*NET does not support prolonged standing for everyone. MRI does not use ionizing radiation but still involves strong magnetic fields, radiofrequency heating, noise, and equipment compatibility risks.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 29-2035.00. BLS OOH provides pay, employment, and outlook for the combined radiologic and MRI technologist category. These findings do not establish mainland Chinese qualifications, licensure, or wage categories.

Check first: physician orders and examination sites, contraindications and safety screening, patient identity and informed communication, coils and imaging techniques, contrast and monitoring requirements, image quality and equipment condition, and abnormality reporting and documentation requirements.

Work cycle: check orders, identity, and institutional screening materials, then complete positioning, image acquisition, monitoring, and quality records under approved protocols. Escalate unclear safety conditions or patient abnormalities under institutional procedures; do not insist on continuing an examination for image quality. Technical quality checks are not disease diagnosis.

Adjacent directions include radiography / CT, nuclear medicine, ultrasound technology, and radiation therapy, each with its own training and qualifications. In the US, a sonographer is an ultrasound technology role and does not automatically correspond to a diagnostic physician in China. MRI experience cannot directly transfer clinical scope or diagnostic report signing authority.

Radiologic technologists handle imaging such as X-rays, fluoroscopy, and CT, while magnetic resonance imaging technologists focus on MRI scanning and image quality. They share foundations in imaging safety and patient communication but use different equipment and physical principles.

Nuclear medicine technologists use radiopharmaceuticals for radionuclide imaging. Magnetic resonance imaging technologists do not use ionizing radiation; imaging principles and safety boundaries differ.

Diagnostic medical ultrasound physicians perform ultrasound imaging and preliminary interpretation. Magnetic resonance imaging technologists operate MRI scanners and ensure image quality; interpretation responsibilities differ.
Radiation therapists deliver radiation treatment according to plans. Magnetic resonance imaging technologists perform diagnostic imaging; work purposes and scopes of practice differ.

US national annual pay for MRI technologists in 2025 at the 10th/25th/50th/75th/90th percentiles was 68890/81040/95480/106340/127670 dollars, with hourly median pay of 45.91. Employment was 43900 in 2025 and is projected to reach 47300 in 2035, with 8% growth during 2025–2035. Annual openings of 2300 include growth and replacement needs and are not a ten-year total.

The 2025 US pay percentiles for the individual MRI occupation have been verified. Percentiles are not starting pay, grades, or take-home income, and must not be spliced with the combined radiologic and MRI median.

Employment was 43,900 in 2025, with 8% growth projected during 2025–2035. Annual openings of 2,300 include replacement needs and are not current recruitment vacancies or annual new jobs. Individual opportunities or AI causation cannot be inferred.
Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, first consider whether you can rigorously conduct patient safety and contraindication screening, communicate patiently with anxious or uncomfortable patients, stand for long periods and operate equipment and displays precisely, check image quality under procedures, and take responsibility for patient safety and image quality. Tools such as RIASEC can only suggest hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.
Positive signals: rigorous safety screening, clear and reassuring patient communication, precise equipment operation and image checks under procedures, and collaboration with medical teams.

Reasons for caution: reluctance to screen strictly for safety, difficulty remaining rigorous under time pressure and patient conditions, discomfort in strong magnetic fields and noisy environments, or inability to follow protection and infection control requirements.

Trial activity: use entirely fictional examination orders and screening checklists to practice contraindication screening, positioning and coil choices, image quality checks, and abnormality reporting. Ask another person to review the records.

The RIASEC interest code is RCI, Realistic–Conventional–Investigative: a preference for operating equipment, executing procedures precisely, and analyzing imaging and safety problems. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

This round obtained no personality validity studies for MRI technologists. Fictional records observe verification and communication habits only and cannot establish fitness for implant safety decisions, medication administration, or clinical operations.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and may be used only for self-reflection.

Entry paths and stages of capability

O*NET's survey of education requirements for new entrants reports 65% associate or two-year degrees, 13% postsecondary certificates, and 9% bachelor's degrees. These are not the qualifications of current workers or mandatory thresholds for all employers. The JobZone3 group training description does not require every MRI technologist to train for one to two years or first gain several years of radiography experience; check ARRT's two pathways separately.

US ARRT MRI certification has primary and postprimary pathways. The former requires an associate degree or higher, recognized MRI education, ethics requirements, and an examination. The latter requires separate checks of supporting discipline credentials, structured education, and clinical experience. Check ARRT certification and state licensure separately; neither automatically confers contrast administration, sedation, or diagnostic authority. This round did not establish a precise nationwide Chinese match for MRI technologist entry and medication authorization. Check health professional technical titles and institutional appointments separately; do not claim there is no unified qualification.

Educational diplomas, professional certification such as certification from the radiologic technologist registry, and state practice licenses are different statuses. Certification does not automatically confer a license or scope of practice. Contrast administration and similar tasks must satisfy the relevant jurisdiction and employer authorization; obtain the required qualifications for the applicable jurisdiction.

Entry stage: practice patient screening and communication, positioning, coil and sequence selection, image quality checks, and documentation under supervision. Learn safety and infection control procedures and keep process records.

Evidence to show: provide a reviewable explanation of examination records, including screening, positioning, coils, image quality checks, and abnormality reporting, to demonstrate the ability to complete MRI examinations under procedures and document truthfully.

Next step: check the target institution's scope of practice, equipment and safety procedures, contrast and monitoring requirements, and validate image quality and patient safety skills during supervised real examinations.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, workers may handle complex sequences and difficult cases, mentor new workers, contribute to quality control and equipment improvements, or move into imaging quality, teaching, and imaging management.
Market signals and transition directions

US O*NET/BLS: employment was 43,900 in 2025 and is projected to reach 47,300 in 2035, with 8% growth during 2025–2035 and 2,300 annual openings from growth and replacement needs. Occupational projections are not current recruitment samples or individual hiring probabilities.
O*NET2025 reports that 94% of MRI technologist employment is in health and social work. This is a US industry employment composition, not China's composition, industry pay, or demand growth.
Transferable capabilities: patient safety and contraindication screening, imaging equipment operation, image quality control, medical communication and teamwork, infection control, and documentation.

Moving into radiologic technology requires additional X-ray / CT physics, radiation protection, target discipline education, and approved clinical experience, plus checks of state licensure and institutional scope. MRI qualifications do not automatically confer radiography, CT, or medication administration authority.

entries.answer: This page covers O*NET 29-2035.00 magnetic resonance imaging technologists: operating MRI scanners, monitoring patient safety, and ensuring image quality. Work includes checking orders, screening for contraindications, explaining procedures and positioning patients, selecting coils and imaging techniques, acquiring images with scanners, administering intravenous gadolinium contrast when needed, connecting physiological monitoring, checking image quality, calibrating equipment, troubleshooting, documenting and reporting, and scheduling appointments. items.answer: In the US, this occupation falls within Job Zone 3 and most jobs require an associate degree. Most states require radiologic technologists to be licensed or certified; a few require MRI technologist licensure. Employers usually require or prefer certification. Certification, licensure, and employer authorization are different, and this page does not assess individual eligibility.

career_risk_cards.heading: Work risks and boundaries for magnetic resonance imaging technologists

risks.consequence: May cause patient injury or equipment damage.
risks.mitigation: Confirm device identity and MR safety status under institutional screening procedures. Check the specific conditions for MR Conditional devices. Do not clear an unknown status based on appearance, removal of carried metal, or past examinations; refer it to the MRI safety lead for review.
risks.scenario: Entering or acquiring images before confirming the MR safety status and applicable conditions for people, objects, or implanted / external devices.

risks.consequence: May cause allergies or adverse reactions.
risks.mitigation: Personnel with the relevant authority must follow orders and medication administration and monitoring systems and check emergency support. MRI certification or employer scheduling does not automatically confer medication administration or sedation authority.
risks.scenario: When contrast is administered without assessment or monitoring.

risks.consequence: May cause falls or interrupted examinations.
risks.mitigation: Reassure the patient and provide immobilization and protection under procedures.
risks.scenario: When the patient is anxious or positioning is insecure.

risks.consequence: May require repeat scans and delay diagnosis.
risks.mitigation: Check image quality against standards and investigate abnormalities.
risks.scenario: When an examination ends without checking image quality.

risks.consequence: May cause infection or occupational exposure.
risks.mitigation: Follow infection control and protection procedures.
risks.scenario: When infection control or protection requirements are not followed.

risks.consequence: May cause thermal injury, hearing damage, or unusable images and require professional handling.
risks.mitigation: Stop the relevant image acquisition under institutionally approved abnormality procedures and notify the responsible person. Stopping scanning does not eliminate the static magnetic field. Do not independently repair, quench, or bypass equipment safety conditions.
risks.scenario: Continuing acquisition despite equipment alarms or patient reports of heating, discomfort, or hearing protection problems.
risks.title: Equipment abnormalities, heating, and hearing risks

factor_rows.answer: US ARRT MRI certification has primary and postprimary pathways. The former requires an associate degree or higher, recognized MRI education, ethics requirements, and an examination. The latter requires separate checks of supporting discipline credentials, structured education, and clinical experience. Check ARRT certification and state licensure separately; neither automatically confers contrast administration, sedation, or diagnostic authority. This round did not establish a precise nationwide Chinese match for MRI technologist entry and medication authorization. Check health professional technical titles and institutional appointments separately; do not claim there is no unified qualification.

description.text: This page covers O*NET 29-2035.00 magnetic resonance imaging technologists: operating MRI scanners for diagnostic imaging, screening for contraindications, positioning patients, selecting coils and imaging techniques, using gadolinium contrast within scope of practice when needed and connecting physiological monitoring, checking image quality, calibrating equipment, documenting, and reporting. To assess this career path, verify the work cycle, patient safety and practice boundaries, evidence scope, risk controls, and observable beginner work samples together.

subject.summary: This page covers O*NET 29-2035.00 magnetic resonance imaging technologists: operating magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners, monitoring patient safety and comfort and ensuring image quality, potentially administering intravenous gadolinium contrast, explaining procedures according to orders, positioning patients, and entering examination data.
